measuredOn: AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D, 16 threads, Fedora 44, headless Chrome for Testing 151.0.7922.169. One run on a quiet desktop, and a fast one. Re-recorded whole after merging phase 5 audit tickets 01 and 03, for ticket 02, which added the three cold-start entries and made the probe reopen the journal after generating the fixture - so every measurement here is taken over that second connection, the way a real boot's reads are, and the numbers it replaces (recorded for phase 5 ticket 05 against the first open, on this same machine) were not comparable to them. Small measurements wobble by tens of percent between runs, which is what the five-times budget in budgets.mjs absorbs. The targets are carried across rather than recorded: what a person can wait for is a judgement, not a measurement. One entry was added after that whole re-recording rather than with it: `search-everywhere` (phase 5 deepening ticket 24), measured at 37ms on this same machine on 2026-09-01 over a query the fixture's non-entry text actually matches, and carrying the target the three entry-search measurements carry, since it is the same screen's wait. `hub-last-writes` was added the same way (phase 8 UX ticket 02), measured at 5ms on this same machine on 2026-09-04 before the hub's live lines were written - which is the order that ticket asks for, since a screen whose reads do not fit is meant to change shape rather than have its budget renegotiated afterwards. The four `mount-*` entries came in with phase 8 audit ticket 01 and are the only ones judged on something other than time: a statement count and a byte count taken at the driver seam, on this same machine on 2026-09-04, because what this architecture pays for a screen is the crossing rather than the query - the whole of Home's 543KB is 33ms of SQLite and a same-process postMessage here, and 543KB of JSON through a serialising bridge on a phone. Their count budgets follow `mountBudgetsFor()` rather than the five-times time rule, and they are seeded at today's numbers deliberately: tickets 13, 14, 16 and 19 each state their acceptance as a reduction in one of these figures, so the budget is the ratchet they tighten rather than a target anybody has agreed. Their `targetMs` is a judgement like every other: 500ms for Home and the stats tab, which assemble a whole screen and already contain reads carrying a 250ms target of their own, and 250ms for the two one-tap screens, which is what `hub-last-writes` already carries. Re-record on the hardware a release is judged against before treating these as the last word: `npm run benchmark:long-journal -- --record` prints this block. `mount-home` was re-recorded on this same machine on 2026-09-05 for phase 8 audit ticket 13, which is the ratchet that ticket tightens: 57 statements and 543KB became 49 and 536KB once Home asked for the facts its tiles draw rather than the lists it reduced. The byte saving reads small here for a reason worth knowing before anyone reads it as a disappointment: 538KB of what is left is one statement, the whole dose log, read inside `stock.getProjections` so the stock panel can count doses per drug since each count was recorded - and this fixture holds no voice benchmarks, 30 measurements and 4 letters, where the audit's own rebuilt journal held 520, 2600 and 60. The reads this ticket narrowed came to 17.7KB here and now come to 10.5KB; on the audit's journal the same three were 524.6KB, 186.0KB and 120.0KB. Narrowing the dose read is a stock ticket, not this one. That ticket is phase 8 audit ticket 26, and it landed: `mount-home` and `stock-projection` were re-recorded on this same machine on 2026-09-05 for it. Home's mount went from 49 statements / 548679 bytes to 49 / 10925 - the statement count deliberately unchanged, because the whole of the saving is one statement changing shape rather than one going away, and `mountBudgetsFor()` leaves the statement ceiling no headroom to absorb a new one. `stock.getProjections` used to ask for every dose logged from the oldest stock count onward and reduce three numbers per drug out of them; it now asks how many non-skipped doses each drug value has in each stretch the attribution can change over, which is one grouped aggregate however long the log is. The 10.5KB the paragraph above predicted for what would be left is what this measures. `stock-projection` fell from 13ms to 2ms for the same reason and its description no longer says the whole dose log, because it no longer reads it. `words-filter-change` came in with phase 8 audit ticket 17 and is the only entry here that times a fold rather than a read: the notes are already in JS by the time a presentation or era filter is tapped, and what the tap costs is the counting over them. It was recorded twice on this same machine on 2026-09-05, over the same fixture and the same run of the benchmark. The before number, 11ms, was taken with the measurement written against the pre-ticket screen - `wordFrequency(notes)` plus a `noteLanguage` walk for the Polish caveat - and the ticket's changes not yet made. The after number, 2ms, is what is recorded above: `countWords` over notes analysed once, with that analysis costing 9ms outside the timer because a tap does not repeat it. Opening the screen therefore costs what it always did and every later tap costs a fifth of it. Two things stop the 11 from being read as the whole of what the ticket removed. Every note in this fixture carries a Polish diacritic, and the language sniff settles on one of those before it tokenises, so the before code made one tokenising pass per note here where a journal written in English made two - the saving on English notes is larger than this pair of numbers shows. And the fixture's notes are built from a 40-word vocabulary, so the counted map is 37 words and the sort is nothing, where a decade of real diary notes is thousands of distinct words. Its target is the 100ms `calendar-month` carries, since both are a control being tapped on a screen already open. `mount-stats` was re-recorded on this same machine on 2026-09-05 for phase 8 audit ticket 16, which is the ratchet that ticket tightens: 66 statements and 781.9KB became 66 and 159.7KB (statements unchanged; two of the mount's reads got smaller, none dropped) once the two interval cards stopped reading the whole journal on every mount. The saving is larger than the ticket's own estimate of 204KB, because that number only ever counted the day-average half of the two cards' cost - dayOfInterval's own dose read, bounded the same way, turned out to be the bigger half on this fixture's 1475 dose events. All four `mount-*` entries were re-recorded again on this same machine on 2026-09-06 for phase 9 audit ticket 12, which found each stale rather than broken: two areas landed after the 2026-09-05 recording above without anybody re-pricing the mounts that ask for them. `documents` (phase 9 features ticket 52) and `appointments` (phase 9 features ticket 57) each registered a `lastWrite.ts` entry, and `assembleLastWrites` asks one bounded MAX per registered area (one `read()` call per entry, run concurrently), so a mount that reads the registry costs exactly one more statement per area added, whichever screen asks - confirmed by tracing the actual SQL crossing the driver seam rather than assumed from the diff. `mount-more-hub` and `mount-coming-back` each cost exactly those two more and nothing else (21 to 23, 33 to 35; the More hub's bytes moved with the new rows, 1245 to 1484, and Coming Back's moved from 19932 to 20171, staying inside its old 21926 budget either way). `mount-stats` costs those same two plus a third: phase 9 features ticket 59 gave chartAnnotations.ts a new source, past appointments drawn on every chart, adding one more statement there alone (66 to 69, 159666 to 165667 bytes - within its old 175633 byte budget on its own, the statement ceiling being the only figure that was ever failing here). `mount-home` costs one, not two, because Home does not read the last-write registry at all - its statement grew for an unrelated reason, phase 9 features ticket 58 giving the debrief offer its own `appointments.getAppointments()` read in place of a hand-set date (49 to 50 statements). That single statement is the whole of the byte growth: 10925 to 16807 is one appointment-table scan, not a regression in anything ticket 26 narrowed - the dose-log read that ticket bounded is untouched.
fixture: seed 1, 3653 days ending epoch day 20676: 3291 entries over 2634 days with entries, 422 photos (393.6MB on disk), 125 lab results, 12 milestones, 24 tags. 265 entries carry a body-region euphoria or dysphoria value. Three regimen episodes (phase 5 ticket 36/38): oral Estradiol from day 30 (Monday/Wednesday/Friday, two-amount schedule, 1475 dose events, 95% of expected slots), Spironolactone for ~500 days in the middle (daily, ends well before the fixture's last 90 days), and injectable Estradiol valerate for the final 150 days (weekly, im) - the last two overlap the first, so a stretch of the fixture has two concurrently active episodes. 19 hair-progress stagings and 5 dated photos. A year each (irregular cadence, ending at the fixture's last day) of measurements, size records, hair-removal sessions, wear sessions and cycle events; a handful of side effects, personal effects, roadmap checks, letters, tryouts and one surgical procedure across the whole decade; ~16 voice recordings; one drug's stock count recorded years ago (so its projection spans the whole dose log, which before phase 8 audit ticket 26 meant reading it) and one recorded near the end (so it doesn't). Encryption on: SQLite3MultipleCiphers under a data key, photos through the encrypting file store.
